blocks.x: I'll make a note on here, we're interviewing Mr. Milton. What is the address here?
St. Anne. And Ralph Collins is here, and Harold Dajon and Bill Russell. Would you mind giving your full name, Mr. Milton?
My name is P. Milton.
And also tell us when you were born, your birthday, and just where it was and all.
June the 14th, 1995, New Orleans. What part of town then?
New Orleans, Louisiana. What part of the town did you come from? Down this section?
Right in this section. Tramway. No, I come from Nightwater.
Nightwater, you come from Nightwater, that's down. Farther downtown. Yeah, because this is a field, Tramway. Did any of your folks play music, your father, mother, or any relatives?
I had a sister play it.
How did she play?
Piano, she played piano.
She older than you?
No, she's younger than me.
Oh, younger. Can you tell us about the first instrument you took up when you started in music?
Well, I already played drum. I always was a drummer, I mean.
How old were you when you started?
Oh, I was about 19 when I started.
You weren't just a little tiny kid then when you started in drums? Oh, no, no, no, no.
Have a regular drum set then?
I have a regular drum set.
Did you take lessons?
No, I didn't take any lessons.
Just picked it up? I wanted to buy it.
Can you tell us about any of the early bands that you heard even before you took up music? Did you ever follow any of the parades or go to some of the dances? Oh, yeah.
I went to many of them.
What were your favorite bands?
The Excelsior Band was my favorite band.
The brass band?
The brass band.
Who was the leader of that at that time?
I think Manny Parash was the leader of that band at that time.
Anybody else in there that you liked? How did you happen to pick out the drums to play?
Well, I just took it up on my own. I mean, I haven't watched anybody really. I just took it up on my own.
I just liked them better than anything else.
That's right.
I mean, no drummer never gave you inspiration to want to play it?
No, no. Just took it out from my own self.
You felt like we ought to play drums?
That's right.
Did you go out and buy yourself a set of drums?
That's right. I bought a set of drums myself.
Yeah, where did you get them?
From Coins, Coins Music Company.
Oh yeah. In Coins.
And it hit Red Coins.
Yeah, I don't remember anything about Coins.
Since you kind of was old prominent, yeah, now. Coranelette, Coranelette, no.
Yeah. Um, can you tell us any about the dance orchestras in those days? Any of the dance orchestras you liked?
Well, I liked the Olympia band. The Olympia band, that was a pretty good band to mine. Who was the leader of that?
Do you remember?
I know all the past. I know all the past. I know all the past.
That's the band Big 8. That's the band Trumbone with.
Oh yeah. Who else is in the, who's the, uh, coronetist in the Olympia band? Do you remember? Cucu. Cucu, with a cow. Oh yeah, a cow.

Not at that time, I don't know. I forgot the fella, but I mean, still, I remember Cucu was playing with him, but. The half of it before Cucu? Oh yeah. I think one time, even Frederick Heppard was in the Olympia, way back. Was there a young Olympia?

I don't know, it seems like. They had two Olympia. I think so. They had the old Olympia and they had the young Olympia. I believe Ricard Alexis told us once that he started out in the young Olympia or something. That's right.

I don't know who was in the man's up there. I think Simon Morera, I think, was managing the young Olympia. Yeah, he was managing the young Olympia band. The bass player. That's right. One, two, one. See, one time, I know, Billy Moran had that band together. They had the Olympia band together. Yeah.
Moran?
Yeah, old man. Eddie Moran, daddy. Oh yeah. Billy Moran. He was calling Billy Moran. He was an old bass player. Oh yeah. In other words, he was doing Mr. Glenny's time, old man Glenny's time. Yeah.
He was the manager of the Superior band too, I think, way back.

That's right. That's right. That's right. But him and I had that band together. I remember that. That's years ago. I mean, that's years ago. Then his son, Simon made a band, a young Olympia. He had two sons playing in that band. John, Marera and Simon. Simon. Simon. Yeah.
What was your drum set like? How many traps and all did you have? A snare and bass drum, anything else? Simple?
This bass drum at that time, I mean, bass drum and snare drum and cymbal at that time.
Have any tom-toms or wood blocks?
No, no. Wood blocks, yeah. Wood blocks, yeah. Wood blocks, yeah.
I had no tom-toms, didn't use no tom-toms in that time. Did you have no bells?
Yeah, car bells, car bells. No tom-toms, didn't use any tom-toms in that time.
Yeah. Did you have any of the hi-hat cymbal ever? Did you?
No, nothing there was no. Sock cymbal? No, there was no wear on. Never. Ain't nobody had nothing like that.
What kind of a foot pedal did you have on that? The same as they make it now?
No, I had overhead when I first saw that overhead. Oh, yeah. Hook it with a strap, I mean. In other words, it was a wood pedal.
Wood pedal. That didn't, that's one of those kind that hit the cymbal at the same time you hit the drum?
That's right, that's right. But you could stop it from hitting the cymbal. I had a piece that you could shove it back and it wouldn't hit the cymbal.
Leave it like a little hammer. If you hit the cymbal, then it wouldn't slowly push it down. Push it back.
You see, if you were 19 when you started, you said it would be about 1914 then, but about the time of the first wars, the world war, it started in Europe.
No, that wasn't that long. I was about 19, that was around 1924, something like that.
When were you born?
June of 14, oh, when I was born, June of 14, 1995. Oh, 1905.
Oh, I see, oh yeah, I had a drum. I didn't hear. Yeah, that would be about 19, in the 1920s then when you started. Yeah.
Right, 1923, 24, seven.
Did you practice by yourself a while or when did you join, when did you join the band?
I made a band out of my own. I made a band out of my own.
Soon after you started? That's right. Who else was in there in a band?

I had the old musicians with me. Really? That's right, I had old man granny, Alphonse Pico, Johnny Dave, Lil' Orange Toker, Gassoun, you remember Gassoun, you got to. I had all old musicians. Lil' Orange Toker and me was the two youngest fellas. I mostly worked with old fellas, I mean when I started, I mean, most old fellas.
And Toker was the carnet player?
The carnet player, he was younger than anybody in the band. He was pretty young.
What band you had, Arnest, when a violin player, what's his name? Oh, Pete, not Pete, uh, Pete. I was playing with you, Tapper's friend. Oh, uh, uh, Dominguez.
Dominguez. Yeah, Paul Dominguez. Paul Dominguez, he worked with me too. What you had in the band with you then, him and whoever? Them Tatt. Tatt, old man granny, Billy, the piano player, Lil' Orange.
Who's the piano player, Billy?
Big Ike, Big Ike Roberson, he was playing with me. Dede, Dede, his wife.
Oh, Billy. Yeah, she played piano with me.
He played. And we had a band together, me and Willie Darren Boyd. We worked at Millen Boyd together.

Lil' Deden Boyd's a violin player, he lived in Batten World. Oh, the Davenport? Darren's Boyd. Darren's Boyd. Oh, Darren's Boyd. That's Caffrey's cousin. Oh, sure, sure. The great band, I'll play Caffrey's cousin. Sure.
Um, did you have a name on that first band? Any just your band? Or did you have any...
Oh, he's in his jazz band.
Where did you play? Remember any of your very first job or where you started out working?
Well, the first job I played in... I can't remember now.
Did you have any long engagement in any certain place?
I went down to Burris and Boydwood most of the time. That's most of the way I played it. Burris, Boydwood, Venus, all that. That was all my work at that time. Boyd, that's all that, I don't know.
Yeah, golf.
I worked down there, Burriside, that was down there mostly. Fishing...
Yeah.

Where they have orange, raised orange. That's right, that's right. I worked at Moreau's a long time. I had a job at Moreau's. We worked out there a long time at Millenburg. Millenburg. Oh, there's Millenburg.
Was that the same first band or that one a little bit later you mentioned?
That was after, that was after, that was after.
That was after.
That was after. That was after.
That was after. That was after. That was after. That was after. That was after. That was after. How late did you play in Millenburg? About what date?
Oh, we played a day a long time. We played a day a long time.
You know about what year it was?
Well, I remember around 19... 2029, something like that. 1929. Did Millenburg last into the depression?
Were there still things going? Do you remember Harold too? Were there... Was there much going on out in the book?

No, there wasn't much going on out there. Our dad, uh, around the depression. You came with me after Eddie Jones and that. After, yeah. But I was at Millenburg before he went there. You see, I was at Millenburg with me, Willard Dennis Boyd. What's that piano player's name? Louis Gallo. Louis Gallo, yeah. And Bill, you see. And then, uh, Bill, uh, then after we left there, then we made, uh, we made a band, and me and Willard Dennis Boyd, then we used to go play out there also. When, uh, around 1929, 30, like that Millenburg was, uh, you know, wasn't much at all. It was on the way down. It was on the way down. Of course, he still had activities out there, but he was on the way out. Yeah. Yeah, he was on the way out.
Yeah, cause Wickwood used to play at Varaday. I'm like Varaday there. Varaday. Hickman and them. Hickman and them.
I was a guy named Dora.
Yeah. But when did that amusement park was that built? Do you remember? I don't know. I found that out there. I went out there to Willie Twenton.

I found that out there. It was? Sure. In those days too? Nothing was out there. I know they had a little amusement park. Remember if they took a ride I showed you on the left-hand side going out where, um, the, um, the, uh, the, uh, the, uh, the neighboring base is there. Yeah. Across from Monroe's house I told you that's where that house all the be where Mowrow used to live. The same one that had the place to live was what he was talking about. Well that's where they had a little amusement park there.
So they had one way back in those days? Yeah.

Things like Ferris Reels? Little Ferris Reels, parties for the chair and the ride, all things like that. Flying horse. I don't remember that next to Baraday. That's right. Because right where we were at the Japanese tea garden, that's where the water started at. Right in front of the side.
That Japanese tea garden was right where the train used to stop. That's right.
That train used to stop right in front. How late did that train run out there do you remember? When they quit that? Was that during the depression? They quit it and they still run
in the streetcars? That was before depression they cut that train off.

Yeah that train was. They cut that way off before depression. I used to go out there to a model T4 and the train wasn't going out there now. That's right. That's right. That's right. The train being cut off. I told you my model T4 was the only thing that
go to the door. Yeah. That's right. That's right. That's right. I knew

even nothing out there. At least the road was not filled that way. No. It was the French one. Gravel roads all the way out there at that time. Gravel roads. I mean you're getting almost there. If you had a good car you couldn't make. You had to have a good model T4. Oh yeah.

That's right. You go walk. Big holes and everything. There was nothing but gravel and old shells. I mean all at Lincoln Beach there was nothing but shells and rocks. I mean it's like you say. I mean you had to have a fold. I mean a real good car couldn't go through there.
You know what I mean? The man he was talking about more on his son. His son was the one that picked my mouth in the Florida. I told him what I was in the band.
Okay. Do you remember some of your other jobs or other bands you played in after after that Melenberg job then? Well I mean I had several bands because I mean on

a little before Buddy Petit. Buddy Petit was playing with me too. He worked with me too. Oh and in your band then? That's right. He was playing second trumpet with me. Buddy Petit. When he died Buddy Petit died on the 4th of July. That he was supposed to go away with me that morning. When I went to his house he was dying. Alright. That's Sunday. That's Sunday. The 4th of July. No he was sick I mean but not he thought he would have been able to make it. When I went there that morning he was dying. When we come back he was late.
Who was the first trumpet?

Lil' Lawrence Toker. Toker. Well he was playing second with me when he died. He was playing my band when he died. He died on the 4th of July. Here in town? Right. Right there. Right on St. Claude and St. Philip.
Do you remember when he died of? What his trouble was? No I know. I never got to know him. I just wondered.

I know he had high fever. I mean when we went there that morning he was just talking about his aid. I mean he wanted to get up. He told his wife, I got to go with that man. I got his deposit. I got to go look like I can see him. I mean when we come back he was late. Because we played the 4th, 5th and 6th of July in Bures. Went to Boerwood for him. Coming back we stopped at Venus. Just less jobs like Bures. Well we took this fella. I don't know if you remember him. He used to call him Jamaica fella. He called him Trap. But he had to rush and get him right away. Trap plates. About stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff stuff like stuff stuff like stuff stuff stuff like stuff stuff
Heard that player?
Yeah, the Jamaica fella. I had to run and get him that morning.
He used to play outdoor halls, and that was Shining Hill.
Oh yeah.
How about some of the house halls you play in?

I play playing halls, I mean like that. Yeah. John Zami and all them halls, I play playing those halls. I play the halls, but you know, not regular jobs, you know what I mean? Yeah, special bands. Off jobs.
You usually had your own band then?

Oh yeah, I mostly worked by myself, mostly all the time. I had plenty of work at that time. I used to give work to every kid right there. Sometimes I had two, three jobs, I used to give them jobs on the side. Wooden Joe worked with me too a while. He worked with me on the last at Moreau. He was the last one worked with me at Moreau. Wooden Joe, Lawrence Morari, and Eddie Johnson. Eddie Johnson was a sacrifice. That was the last one when the place closed. They had added.
Yeah.

That was the last one worked with me after. Wooden Joe and Lawrence Morari. Sometimes he'd send Willie O'Connell in his place. I mean, in other words, he would work three nights a piece. One would work four nights, one a week, that one would make three nights.
Willie O'Connell is representative of the union in Beluxian, huh? Well, what does he play? Carlet? No, banjo.
Oh, Lawrence then.
One of your good banjo players.
Yeah, Willie O'Connell. He used to live with Lawrence, remember when he was living with Lawrence, I mean.
Yeah, and you worked out there at the morrows every night then?
Every night. We was playing at there every night. Yeah, we were there.
Maybe just weekends. You usually go out on Sunday going out on Sunday.
No, we were waiting at seven nights. Oh, every night in the picnic on Sunday. Yeah, Sunday, that's right. Every night. We played dead picnics and played at night.
Yeah, I always hear about these picnics. That was in the all day long, was it? Yeah, all day long.
Then we had to start playing at night for him. I mean, he'd have special picnics then we had to start playing at night.
Yeah. What hours did you have out there at night time about?
We played at 8 to 12, I believe you should work out there.

Yeah, work out there at 8 to 12. Sometimes, you see, at that time, if the man had a good crowd, you stayed there maybe in that hour. That's right. No, no, overtime. Sometimes he'd give you something, you know. Sometimes, well, there's not much you better knock off.
If you have a crowd, he'd tell us to stay there. Yeah.
Well, then you'd get paid extra for the stay. No. Sometimes, but soon when you have a good or a bad night, you leave you off the toilet. That's right. You'd still have the same thing? Sure.
The kitty though, you'd make money in the kitty.

Yeah, you'd make good money in the kitty, you see? Yeah, it'd be worth staying. Yeah, it'd be worth staying because he'd always, to make you feel good, he'd always come put some in it. That's right. Yeah, you know. Did they ever have pianos out there at the lake in those camps?
They had a piano next door to us, Walter DeCue was playing. That was the name of the place next to Moro. No, not the Stoops. Right next to Moro. Yeah. Walter DeCue was playing piano.

I don't remember the name, but I know what you mean. I can show you. I can show you right now. I forgot the name. I really forgot the name of it. They had a... But it wasn't far from us. I mean, we could look at them, I mean, from where they was, it's about half a block. We could look at them, I mean, through the screen playing, they could look at us. At that time, Walter DeCue and... Walter DeCue and... The Dugard, the Dugard, they used to play drums, Red Dugard. They was out there at that time. Them's all old, old musicians, what I'm talking about. You heard of Red Dugard?
Oh yeah.
Yeah.
They was all old musicians.

Well, people have told us that the music sounded prettier or louder or something over the water. Do you think it made any difference? When you'd hear it across the water, did it ever... Did it seem to carry any better?
It was sounding better from forth. It was sounding better from forth. You could hear it plainer that way over the water than you would over land? Yeah. That's right.
I never did have the...
If it was a quiet night, you could hear it a long, long way off.
You hear it a long way and it takes a good while getting to it.
That's right. It sounds like...
You take it right across you, but you're getting there all the time.

It sounds close to what it is. The beat sounds close to what it is, you see. Yeah. That might be about five, six blocks you think if maybe right there and you get to walk and wave for him what you thought he was.

Can you tell us anything about the different trumpet players you worked with, like Buddy Petit? I never got to hear him. What style he played? Could you give any idea what he played like or any other... He was a nice...
He was a nice trumpet player, Buddy was a nice... In other words he had a different tone I think than any of those trumpet players.
He wasn't too much of a loud trumpet player but he had a sweet tone. I mean, he wasn't those blasted, you know what I mean, blasted trumpet.

He was a... In other words he was a better second man than he was a first trumpet, you know what I mean. Of course he used to play first in his band but I mean he was a better second trumpet player. Did he need any music for those, when he'd sit in with Tolka, play with him, did he ever have the parts or anything, just make them up? No. No. No. No. No. No. No. He wasn't there with stuff there with stuff there with stuff He was just a soft trumpet player. I mean, what he'd make out that old, I mean, he's just a good trumpet player. He was good. One of the best second trumpet players I believe they had here.
Did he read music? Was he able to read music all right? Did you ever see him use arrangements with his own band?
No, I have never. I've never seen any music.
Did he play mostly open horn or use any mutes or hat or anything of that kind?

He used hat mutes. I mean, he'd play open. I mean, he'd play the sweet horn. I mean, he'd play the sweet horn. If you'd get to hear him, you'd know him any way he's at. I mean, he just had a different tone than those other fellas. I mean, there wasn't no blasted trumpet player.
How did he compare with Louis Armstrong, for instance? Was it anything like that or different?
No, Louis had a more rougher tone than Buddy had. I mean, it was a soft trumpet player.
Yeah.
It was a soft trumpet player.
How did he compare with Kid Rene? I never got the...I heard Kid Rene once at the very end when he was...
Well, Rene was on the Art of Louis Armstrong.
He was more like Louis Armstrong.
He was more on the Art of Louis Armstrong. Yeah.
I heard...
Punch all of them, I mean, they were very nice compared like the same. But Buddy was different than him. He played a soft horn in them. I mean, he had a different style in them altogether.
Did he have any special favorite pieces or anything that he was specialized in, any certain numbers?
Well, he was like the Tiger Rag and different thing. I mean, all numbers like that, I mean.
Did you ever play with Chris Kelly? I've heard about him. He's another...
I played with Chris Kelly a couple of jobs, I mean. But I left him. I mean, I didn't like his ways. I left him. I didn't stay with him.
How was his style? Was it anything like either Armstrong or like Buddy Batista?
No, no, no, no. He's... He had his own style, him. He had his own style. I've heard he was very good in the blues.
He's good.

He was good. That's what he was bad on, blues than anything. He was bad on blues than anything. In other words, I believe he was one of the best blues trumpet players that he had. I mean, that's mostly what he used to do, blues mostly.
Did he use a lot of mutes? Chris Kelly?
No, he mostly used his hat, him and his hand, you know what I mean? Well, he's just a youth that are taller than the other one. Yeah, that and flush that.
The rubber plunger thing, yeah.

At that time when he had a bigger band, what you call him used to mostly lead these bands, Ricard. Remember when him and Ricard had a band together? That was before we got stuck playing bass. He used to lead the band.
I knew he played trumpet in the old days. I heard him once in a parade. He's a nice trumpet player.
Yeah, that's what I heard. Nice trumpet player.
Boy, you had a job, brother. That's right.
He sure was.
Can you tell us anything about Wooden Joe in the old days? I heard Wooden Joe from about 1943 on.
Wooden Joe is one of the powerful trumpet players you had here.
He was very powerful even when I heard him in the last stage.

He was one of the powerful that you had here. You'd be in a parade, you could hear him, if you didn't hear nothing else, you'd hear him. That's where he got that name, Wooden Joe. I mean, he was powerful. Wooden Joe. I never heard nobody blow louder than him yet. I mean, real, the facts. He was the loudest you ever heard. That's right.
He was about the loudest I ever heard.

He stood up to that name too. They'd say Wooden Joe. That's where he got that name, from Wooden Joe. And he played with you out at the Lake of Middleburg. That's the last one worked with him at the... Littlewoods. Littlewoods. Littlewoods. Littlewoods. That's the last one worked at me, Littlewoods. Littlewoods.
I remember a few years ago, Kid Clayton was out there in Littlewoods and a couple of other places.

He was my Mama Lou's. He was at Mama Lou's. You know, he even passed there. He was my Mama Lou's. He was at Mama Lou's, yeah. When did Lincoln Beach start? He was more close, I mean, in town. Well, I worked at Happa Landon a long time too. I worked with Georgie Park out there a long time.
This was ten years ago. I heard music.
He was a Georgie Park piano player. Yeah. I worked with him a long time, I think.
I used to hear some music farther on, around the lake. Must be where Lincoln Beach is now. It was a long time ago, though.

Yeah, well, see, along them camps. They had music all over at that time. Every night, you see, that four or five camps had bands every night, but on weekends, most of every camp along that lake had bands. And then when you leave, well, Lincoln Beach is going to one little river all out there. They had picnics, you know, parties. Oh, man, music was good. Yeah.

Yeah. All you had to do is blow a horn a long time ago. You'd get work, I mean, because they didn't have that many musicians like they got now, you see. But all them little fellas now, they want to be musicians before they're long. They want to go play, you see. They didn't like that time before you had trouble. I mean, sometimes find musicians. But there's so many jobs, they ain't had enough musicians.
Some of them could play twice, but they play now.
Yes, yes.
Good friends, God, glory, no.
Yeah. Well, how was the Whitman Joe as a musician? Did he know all the horn real well and different keys? Was he able to read? No, I never did know. I heard him a few times.
Well, for my life, he reads some posts, I mean, that I know of. I wouldn't say he was one of the greatest, but I know he could read it, you know what I mean?
Handle arrangements and all them do.

Well, I'm going to tell you, I never did see them food and arrangements. At that time, them fellas didn't food and all the arrangements. Never used them in the Althera Collagen. No, they didn't have food and arrangements at that time. See, mostly now, I mean, the band's bigger now, they used arrangements. A long time ago, they didn't have food and arrangements. I mean, they played what they know, I mean. Some orchestration just would bite them up bad enough.
Yeah.
That's right, see.
Can you remember any other jobs you had during the Depression, after 1930, along in there? After you closed out at the lake, at Millenburg?
I played several different jobs, I mean. It's hard to think of them, played so many of them. I went down to Buress a long time.
All through your career, yeah. What played you played at Buress most? Huh? I played Buress, Venus. I mean, who you played for at Buress most? Rex Club or Buck Jones or?

I know the name, all I know where they was. I mean, I never knew their name. See, none of them fellas, people didn't carry no name at their club at that time like they do now, you know. All they tell you they got a job in Buress, I mean, they put no name on no contract or nothing. They tell you Buress, I mean. I went down there so long, I just couldn't know where it was by heart, I mean. There was no other place to play, it was better than Chauvin. Yeah. They had a funny name there, yeah. Funny name they called them, I mean. A long time ago, they never had no name, I mean, like they got now, I mean, like the Star Club and all that, like they got all out there. They didn't, they didn't had that.
Well, whoever is going to play, I said, where are you going? I'm going to play for Mr. Soil.

Yeah. Felice, come on, Felice, Felice was in Buress, I mean, that's, you know, that was going to play for him. John Rowell, I mean, at Sunrise, you know. It was just, say the name who was going to play for it, so people would know.
What sort of music did they like down there? Was it regular Dixieland type or whatever you want to call it?
Dixieland and jazz, I mean.
I didn't know if a lot of the people started Cajuns or what they are down there, if they liked it.
Well, I got Free Jacks, I mean, whatever you call them.
But they played the same kind of music there?

All the time, I mean, that's what they wanted. I mean, you couldn't go down with no Chitterbug like they do now down there. They didn't go for that. You go down there and now you play that kind of music. That's right. Yeah, certain ones you had to play that.
Yeah, like that Dixieland and jazz.
And they'll ask you too, if they call you, I mean, do you play Dixieland and jazz? Some of them placed down there, you said, no, they don't want you.
No. You go down there every week then?
Every Friday, every Saturday we go down there.
Just the local people, wouldn't it be people from here sometime go down or tourists or what kind of crowd did you have?

They had their own crowd. They had their own crowd. They would come from different sections, you know, Venus. People from Burst would come to Venus, I mean, and Potash, all them different places down there. I mean, they'd come there. They know New Orleans people all there. They're selling them.
Most of the people come from, say, from where they're from, all the time, all the time, all the time. Yeah, all the time, all the time. Like that.
But are they mostly down there trappers or fisher rooms?
Fisher, trappers and...
People like that.
Food and more. Artists and that, all the things like that. Yeah. The old people that have money, I mean, they pay $2, $3 to come in the dance.
The regular dance is a charge to get in charge at the door and then to get in. That's right. I know they still have music. They have an orange festival. I've been wanting to go down every year.
They got some, I know who's going down there, but they got some bands going down there. I know who's going down there.
Andy Anderson went about a year ago, I know. He was going down there.

Andrew Anderson. I played with, I played with them. Trumpet players. I forget who else was in the band. I worked in Delacue Island too. I worked down there. But not, not, not regular. I worked down there a couple of nights, I mean.
